claims.text: SPS can rapidly consolidate a mechanically alloyed mixture of refractory metals and Cu while driving an in-situ reaction.
The in-situ reaction can overcome thermodynamic segregation caused by the positive heat of mixing between Cu and refractory elements.
The proposed process can produce a large-scale composite with a refined and stable microstructure.
The starting material is a blended powder containing refractory alloying elements and dispersed Cu particles.
The powder blend is processed by SPS using rapid heating and cooling, elevated pressure, and an inert atmosphere.
A suitable SPS processing-temperature range is 1400–1700 °C.
A uniaxial pressure of approximately 30 MPa is suitable for the SPS process.
Short SPS dwell times limit diffusion.
Fine intermetallic, ceramic, or other reaction products form in situ as evenly dispersed reinforcements.
The dispersed reaction products arrest coarsening of Cu-rich regions.
Rapid heating and high pressure during SPS induce fast densification.
The short diffusion time limits detrimental effects of the positive mixing enthalpy between Cu and refractory elements.
SPS promotes a controlled in-situ reaction that produces a fine and uniform microstructure.
Interfacial reaction products remain confined to the nanoscale.
Nanoscale interfacial reaction products provide effective bonding between the refractory and Cu phases.
The resulting composite will have a uniform, fine-grained microstructure and well-bonded refractory/Cu interfaces.
The SPS-processed composite will have enhanced mechanical properties relative to conventionally processed counterparts.
The SPS-processed composite will have enhanced thermal stability relative to conventionally processed counterparts.
Conventional casting or slow sintering generally produces phase segregation and coarse, unstable microstructures because of prolonged high-temperature exposure and diffusion.
Excessive heating duration or improper pressure control may cause segregation or deleterious phase formation.
